clinicalPearls: A recognisable pattern of ocular, dental and digital anomalies caused by variants in GJA1, encoding the gap junction protein connexin-43
The hand hallmark is type III syndactyly, characteristically fusion of the fourth and fifth fingers, sometimes with camptodactyly
Ocular features include microphthalmia, microcornea and a narrow palpebral fissure, with a risk of glaucoma
Enamel hypoplasia and small, malformed teeth are typical, alongside a thin nose with hypoplastic alae and a narrow nasal bridge
Usually autosomal dominant; neurological problems including spasticity and white matter changes can emerge, sometimes progressively
The combination of syndactyly, small eyes and dental anomalies with a distinctive nose is highly suggestive
Management is supportive with ophthalmic surveillance (including for glaucoma), dental care and monitoring for neurological features
reference.pathophysiology: Oculodentodigital dysplasia is caused by variants in GJA1, which encodes connexin-43, a component of gap junctions that permit direct intercellular communication. Impaired connexin-43 channel function disrupts coordinated signalling between cells in developing eyes, teeth, digits, bone and neural tissue. This explains the pleiotropic phenotype of microphthalmia and glaucoma risk, enamel hypoplasia, syndactyly and craniofacial features, as well as the later neurological manifestations attributable to disturbed gap-junction communication in the central nervous system.
additionalDifferentials: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (dental and craniofacial features)
additionalInvestigations: GJA1 sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Ophthalmic assessment including intraocular pressure and screening for glaucoma
Hand and skeletal radiographs to characterise syndactyly and bone changes
Dental assessment for enamel hypoplasia and tooth anomalies
Neurological evaluation and brain MRI where neurological features are present
Family evaluation given autosomal dominant inheritance
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure or established glaucoma threatening vision
Progressive spasticity, gait disturbance or other neurological decline
Significant visual impairment from microphthalmia or associated anomalies
Functional impairment of the hands from severe syndactyly
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is generally normal, but vision is at risk from glaucoma and ocular anomalies, and a subset develop progressive neurological problems, so long-term ophthalmic and neurological follow-up is advisable.
pitfalls: Missing glaucoma because intraocular pressure is not routinely monitored
Treating the syndactyly in isolation without recognising the broader syndrome
Overlooking evolving neurological features that may appear years after diagnosis
Failing to examine and counsel apparently mildly affected relatives
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; care is supportive and coordinated across specialties
Ophthalmic surveillance for glaucoma with intraocular-pressure-lowering therapy or surgery, and correction of refractive and microphthalmia-related problems
Restorative dental care for enamel hypoplasia and small malformed teeth
Hand surgery to correct type III syndactyly and improve function
Neurological surveillance for emerging spasticity and white-matter disease, with physiotherapy and antispasticity agents as needed
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant GJA1 variant with family evaluation
Long-term multidisciplinary follow-up given the progressive potential of ocular and neurological features
